This week's consumer confidence report showed the share of consumers saying jobs are “plentiful” rose to 30.8% from 26.2%, the highest of 2026, while “hard to get” fell to 18.4% from 21.4%, the lowest of 2026. 

The gap between them, at +12.4, is the widest since mid-2025 per Bloomberg, and more than four times July’s low of +2.7.

https://pro.thestreet.com/market-commentary/consumer-confidence-jumps-to-highest-since-january-2025-beating-every-estimate
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
𝗦&𝗣 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗙𝗹𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗨𝗦 𝗣𝗠𝗜𝘀 (𝗡𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿)
Composite 54.6 (October 55.9)
Manufacturing 54.5 (est 54.6; October 54.9)
Services 54.7 (est 55.8; October 56.1)

Growth cooled to the slowest since July but stayed solid, with S&P calling it “sustained strong economic growth.”

Activity and demand:
▪️ Composite at a four-month low; manufacturing PMI at a three-month low, still improving for a 16th straight month; services at a four-month low.
▪️ New orders grew at the weakest pace since July, “led by a marked slowing of new business inflows into the service sector” on uncertainty, high prices and higher interest rates.
▪️ Exports fell for the first time in four months.

Capacity:
▪️ Backlogs rose again in both manufacturing and services on “constrained operating capacity.”
▪️ Hiring was “the joint-third largest seen for over four years,” with factory job creation “the second-strongest since July 2021.”
▪️ Supplier delivery times lengthened the most since August 2022, tied to “global trade disruptions,” especially for metals and electronics.

Prices:
▪️ Selling price inflation cooled after October’s rise, the largest since August 2022, with “manufacturing selling prices rising especially sharply.”
▪️ Input cost inflation eased for a second month, “helped by lower fuel prices,” but stayed above the year-to-date average.
▪️ Bloomberg noted price gauges “rose at the slowest pace since August but were still elevated.”

Sentiment “revived from October’s five-month low” on “hopes of reduced political instability following the midterm elections,” though manufacturing confidence fell on costs, supply and tariff uncertainty.

S&P Global’s Chris Williamson said the surveys “still point to GDP rising at an annualized rate of about 3% in the fourth quarter,” but “the survey price gauges remain at levels consistent with inflation running well above the Fed’s 2% target in the coming months,” and expectations “clearly remain subdued by historical standards.”

BREAKING: The US goods trade deficit widened by -$14.6 billion in October, or -10.8%, to -$149.5 billion, its 3rd-widest monthly gap on record.

This marks the 4th consecutive monthly increase in the shortfall, totalling -$48.4 billion.

Goods imports soared +$21.1 billion, or +6.1%, last month, to a record $365.3 billion.

This was driven by imports of capital goods, which include computers and accessories, semiconductors, and telecommunications equipment powering the AI buildout, which jumped +8.5%.

At the same time, exports of goods increased +$6.7 billion, or +3.2%, to $215.8 billion, the 2nd-highest on record.

The US trade deficit is widening sharply.

US semiconductor stocks are seeing nearly unprecedented volatility:

On Tuesday, the Semiconductor Index, SOX, underperformed the Nasdaq 100 by 5.9 percentage points, its 4th-biggest daily underperformance on record.

This was exceeded only in 2 trading sessions in 2000 and one in January 2025.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis, the largest daily underperformance of SOX was 4.7 percentage points.

On Wednesday, SOX outperformed the Nasdaq 100 by 7.2 percentage points, its largest daily outperformance since January 2001.

So far in November, semiconductor stocks have underperformed the Nasdaq 100 by 8.2 percentage points, following an 8.7 percentage point underperformance in October.

Rarely has there been volatility like we are seeing now.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
The most important assumption in the SALP letter is that RSI creates an oligopoly at the frontier with real pricing power. TLDR; market structure at the frontier might be the single most important variable for tech investing over the next 2-3 years. 

If the model layer is more competitive, then intelligence will be priced closer to cost and the surplus will flow to compute, customers and incumbents with real distribution rather than the labs. And obviously many of the incumbents mentioned in the letter would then thrive rather than die. Simply said, the better that Anthropic and OpenAI do vs. other model competitors, the worse it is for almost every other company on earth especially AI infra and especially apps.

On balance, I do think that Neon - and the overall recent pace from GDM - cuts against many of the more extreme assumptions in the letter. The risk for OpenAI and Anthropic is that a vertically integrated lab with much lower compute costs clearly reaches the frontier before they successfully vertically integrate.

New releases from Gemini, Muse, Grok and the forthcoming larger training runs from American open-source labs like Reflection, Thinking Machines and of course Nvidia are big cards that we will turn over in the next few months. Especially Nvidia given they are the “trainer of last resort.”

“Gemini Distillation Services” are very interesting in this context. Makes one wonder why Microsoft is not fully open-sourcing given their recent acceleration in perplexity gains from pre-training. 

And of course, OpenAI’s last financing round looks like a mistake as Anthropic probably needs to be worth over $3 trillion for OpenAI to be vaguely financeable and they will need a financing in the next 15 months. But so many strategics have an incentive to help OpenAI that unlikely to be a real issue. Can probably “grow” into the valuation with some help from strategics.

SALP letter was great btw. Leopold is a very smart, resilient guy with incredible connectivity in the SF AI community. Also noteworthy that they have increased headcount by roughly 50% since June 30th given their views on AI. Humans might turn out to have a longer shelf life than expected. 

Fluid intelligence per watt FTW. For now.

🪙Lots of eyes on USD1 overnight after briefly depegging. Here is a look from @TheTerminal stablecoin dashboard: 

The supply chart is worth a look. Circulating supply is $2.72B, and the slide started well before last night:

• Supply last peaked near $4.47B on Oct. 6. It's down about $1.75B, or 39%, in under eight weeks.

• November has done most of the damage: roughly $1.15B gone this month, a 30% drop.

• After a week of holding steady around $2.85B, supply fell about $129M today (4.5%), the largest one-day decline in the past six months.

• From the June high of $4.85B, it's down 44%.

Burns are outpacing mints.

Yesterday I released The 2027 Macro Outlook to MACROSHARK members.

This one was a labor of love. The result is 85 pages, more than 20,000 words and over 80 charts on where we are in the cycle, where liquidity goes next and how I think the year plays out.

People like to say macro is a puzzle. It most certainly is. You're trying to put the pieces together to see the complete picture.

But I think of it more like a Rubik's Cube. Solve one side and you can scramble another. Very rarely do all six sides line up at once. When they do, conditions are aligned for something good to happen.

I think 2027, much like 2026, will be a year of two halves. And the cube may end up showing all its sides at once... but that's more a story for the second half than the first.

I'm proud of it, and I hope members get as much out of reading it as I did out of writing it.
